down.origin: Down is the soft plumage that grows beneath the contour feathers of waterfowl, in commerce principally domestic geese (Anser anser domesticus and related domestic forms) and ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus). Most commercial down is recovered from birds raised for meat and collected at slaughter. A smaller share has been harvested from live geese, a practice the European Food Safety Authority examined in 2010 at the European Commission's request. Down quality depends on species, bird age and maturity, and processing, so origin and species claims need documentation.
down.structure: A down cluster is a plumule: a feather without a stiff vane, in which many soft barbs radiate from a small base and carry fine barbules. The barbules lack the hooklets that zip contour feather vanes together, so the barbs stay separate and form a three-dimensional, springy cluster that traps still air. In their review of feather morphogenesis, Alibardi and Toni describe the barbs of downfeathers as forming independently, and identify the dominant structural protein as feather keratin, a small protein of about 10 kDa that replaces alpha-keratins in barb and barbule cells and polymerizes into filaments by a mechanism different from mammalian hair keratin.
down.process: Down and feathers are collected at slaughter or, where permitted, gathered from live birds during molt. The raw material is washed with detergents to remove dirt and preen oil, rinsed, dried at high temperature to sanitize it, cooled, and then separated by air-flow sorting, in which air currents lift the lighter down clusters away from heavier feathers, fragments and dust. Blends are then made to a target specification such as a stated down to feather ratio, tested for composition, cleanliness and fill power, and blown into baffled or sewn-through shells.
down.performance: Dry, lofted down gives very high warmth for its weight compared with most fiber fillings, compresses into a small volume and recovers repeatedly. Fill power, the volume a fixed mass occupies after standardized conditioning and compression (expressed in cubic inches per ounce in US practice), is the usual loft index. Its main weakness is moisture: wet clusters collapse and lose insulation, and drying is slow, which led to hydrophobic down treatments. Down is protein, so strong alkali and chlorine bleach damage it, and soiled down can support insects and odor. Fill power results from different test protocols are not directly comparable.
down.identify: Burn tests (indicative only; perform with care) show keratin behavior but reveal nothing about species or grade. Laboratories assess fill by hand-sorting a weighed sample into categories such as down clusters, down fibers, feathers, broken feathers and residue, and use microscopy of barbule structure to separate goose from duck. Frequent problems are duck sold as goose, overstated down percentages, and feather fragments counted as down. Live-plucking cannot be detected in the finished fill, so welfare claims rest on audited supply-chain records.
down.labeling: Composition and loft claims are tested under industry methods such as the IDFB testing regulations and European standards, including EN 12130 for fill power. Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires textile products containing non-textile parts of animal origin to state this on the label. Textile Exchange's Responsible Down Standard is a voluntary certification that prohibits live-plucking and force-feeding and tracks certified down through the chain of custody. EFSA's 2010 opinion distinguished gathering ripe feathers during molt, which can be done without pain, from plucking, which causes bleeding follicles and other injury.
down.past: Down and feathers have long been used as bedding and quilt fillings, and industrial washing and air sorting later turned them into a graded commodity for bedding and outdoor clothing. Concern about harvesting feathers from live geese led the European Commission to request a scientific opinion from EFSA, which held a stakeholder meeting in May 2010, received 922 submissions in a public consultation, and adopted its opinion on 27 October 2010. EFSA concluded that at least minor pain and injury seemed unavoidable under commercial conditions if plucking occurred, and recommended removing only ripe feathers with a control system, a position later reflected in voluntary down standards.

feather.origin: Feathers used in fillings are mainly the small body and contour feathers of domestic ducks and geese, recovered with down during processing. Far larger tonnages of chicken feathers come from poultry processing; these are not normally used as filling but are an abundant keratin by-product studied for fibers, composites and other materials. Decorative feathers come from farmed birds and, historically and in some regions still, from wild species, whose trade is restricted for many birds by wildlife law and by CITES.
feather.structure: A contour feather has a hollow basal calamus that sits in the skin, continuing as the rachis, which bears barbs; the barbs carry barbules with tiny hooklets that interlock to form a flat vane. Alibardi and Toni describe how barb ridges fuse during growth to produce the rachis and vane, whereas in down the barbs stay independent. Feathers are built mainly from feather keratin, a small protein of about 10 kDa that shares a core-box motif with reptilian scale proteins and is resistant but not very elastic. In fillings, the curvature of the shaft supplies spring, and the stiff quill is why feathers can poke through lightweight fabrics.
feather.process: Filling feathers follow the down route: washing to remove dirt and oils, drying and sanitizing at high temperature, and air-flow sorting that separates feathers by size and weight from down clusters. Smaller, curved feathers are preferred for pillows and cushions, and feather-rich blends are specified by their down to feather ratio. Industrial poultry feathers are processed differently, for example hydrolyzed or dissolved to extract keratin. Reddy (2015) notes that poor thermoplasticity and the difficulty of dissolving feather keratin have limited its use in fibers and composites despite low cost and abundance.
feather.performance: Feathers provide springy, supportive loft rather than the high insulation of down, and they tolerate repeated compression in cushions. Their quills can migrate through covers, so tightly woven, down-proof ticking is used. Like down, feathers lose loft when wet and are protein-based, so they are harmed by alkali and chlorine and can harbor dust mites and odor if not kept clean and dry. Decorative feathers are fragile, fade in light and are vulnerable to insect pests in collections.
feather.identify: Burn tests (indicative only; use precautions) show keratin behavior. In fill analysis, feathers are separated from down by hand-sorting a weighed sample into categories such as whole feathers, broken feathers and quill fragments. Microscopy of barbules and their nodes can help identify bird groups, which is useful when checking species claims in fillings and when assessing decorative objects that may contain feathers of protected species.
feather.labeling: Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 does not treat feathers as a textile fiber, and textile products that contain non-textile parts of animal origin must state this on the label. In the US, filling composition claims fall under general FTC truth-in-advertising law and are commonly tested against industry methods. Trade in feathers of native wild birds is restricted in the US by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and internationally many bird species are listed by CITES, so their feathers require permits for international trade.
feather.past: Feathers have served as bedding, insulation and adornment across many cultures. In the late nineteenth century the millinery trade in plumes from egrets and other wild birds drove severe declines and prompted early bird-protection campaigns, which fed into US laws such as the Lacey Act of 1900 and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Today much research on feathers concerns the poultry industry's by-product stream: reviews of keratin extraction and feather applications describe hydrogels, films, fibers and composites, while noting that scale-up remains limited.
